source.title: Compute-Optimal LLMs Provably Generalize Better with Scale
source.authors: Marc Finzi; Sanyam Kapoor; Diego Granziol; An-Ming Gu; Christopher De Sa; J. Kolter; Andrew Gordon Wilson

record.tranche_reason: The study uses Chinchilla compute-optimal scaling as an assumption and selects Pythia checkpoints along that frontier, but its main results concern generalization bounds rather than testing the claim versions about held-out loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates generalization-bound components and reports an empirical-loss curve, but does not evaluate held-out pretraining loss or test whether smaller-run fits predict larger runs. It assumes the Chinchilla allocation rather than testing it. The empirical-loss curve is for training data and is shown without per-checkpoint values in the text; cited scaling-law results are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study assumes the Chinchilla compute-optimal ratio (N/D ≈ 1/20) and uses it to pick Pythia checkpoints and derive asymptotics. Its own results concern generalization-bound components: loss variation, quantization gap and prequential information content. It reports no held-out loss scaling fit, extrapolation test, allocation estimate, shape comparison or downstream results, so no claim version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that compute-optimal LLMs have generalization bounds that tighten with scale. This is because the parameters-per-token ratio stays constant while loss variance and quantization error fall. Prequential coding shows model information growing sublinearly, which implies a shrinking generalization gap. They present a scaling law for the generalization gap but do not test the loss scaling laws themselves.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops empirical martingale generalization bounds and evaluates their components; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The two smallest Pythia points are interpolated because their checkpoints have too-small N/D; the 12B checkpoint is excluded because it failed to quantize properly.

fits_no_version.finding: The token-wise loss variation Σ on Pythia compute-optimal checkpoints decreases with parameters, fitted as 0.27 + 8337·N^-0.54 (Fig. 2 center).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-token loss variation of compute-optimal LMs shrinks roughly as 1/√N toward a constant floor.

fits_no_version.finding: Prequential-coding upper bound on model information content scales as about 6×10^5·N^(0.5±0.1). It is predicted to fall below parameter-counting bits near 20–30B parameters (Fig. 3 left).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The information content of compute-optimal LMs grows sublinearly with model and dataset size.

fits_no_version.finding: The evaluated token-wise generalization bound decreases with scale on Pythia, both quantization-based and prequential-based (Figs. 2 left, 3 right). The 4-bit GPTQ quantization gap also shrinks with size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization-gap bounds for compute-optimal LMs tighten predictably with scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Training empirical risk falls across the Pythia compute-optimal checkpoints (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training empirical risk decreases along the Pythia compute-optimal checkpoint series.

record.problems: The empirical-loss result is training risk rather than held-out risk, and the paper reports no per-checkpoint values for that curve in the text. The largest model was excluded from the quantization-based evaluation after quantization failed; the two smallest checkpoints were interpolated. The study evaluates bounds and their components rather than directly measuring a train-test generalization gap.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for loss variation, quantization gap, or the generalization bound: these are components or outputs of the paper's bound analysis, not measurements of the behaviors named by the claim versions. Hessian-spectrum and prequential-coding analyses likewise do not test those versions.

untested.parts: Held-out loss is not measured, and no power law is fitted to loss versus N, D or C.
No extrapolation from small-run fits to larger runs is tested against measured loss.
The Chinchilla allocation (a=b=0.5, G²≈1/20 from Besiroglu et al.) is assumed, not estimated.
No other modalities or training regimes.
No test of how fitting or setup choices change exponents or the compute-optimal split.

record.verdict_notes: The Chinchilla law is used as an assumption: for checkpoint selection (N/D = G² ≈ 1/20) and for the asymptotic O(D^(1-β)) derivation. The power-law fits reported (Σ and K(h)) are for bound components, not for pretraining loss. The rows_left_out justification is reasonable; the bound-component findings are recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute. It shows training empirical risk across checkpoints.
No test of whether power-law fits from small runs predict substantially larger runs.
The compute-optimal allocation is assumed for selecting checkpoints; the study does not measure how optimal parameter and token counts vary with compute.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests across other modalities or training regimes.
No investigation of how fitting choices alter scaling exponents or the compute-optimal split, and no test for departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: Pythia compute-optimal checkpoints
rows.size_stated: 70 million to 12 billion parameters; the 12B checkpoint was removed from this evaluation
rows.operation_detail: Compared empirical training risk across checkpoints selected along the compute-optimal frontier.

conditions.value: The two smallest models were linearly interpolated using N/D; the 12B model was excluded after quantization failed

rows.measure: Empirical risk R̂h (training negative log likelihood)
rows.value: figure only; the text says empirical loss improves as the model is scaled up
rows.note: The curve is shown for the checkpoint series; the text provides no per-checkpoint loss values or fitted power law. This is training empirical risk, not held-out loss.
rows.check: The row is training-set empirical risk on Pile (IID token subsample of 10^4), not held-out loss. It is shown only in Figure 2 left, with no values or power-law fit. The 12B model was excluded and the 70M/160M points were interpolated. It cannot bear on V1, which needs held-out loss following a power law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
